title: Kestrel and the Confession
premise: Estate lawyer Kestrel Villalobos is summoned to probate the will of Aldous Merrick, a client who died a year ago — yet the will is dated three days after his death, and it names her executor. Twin letters arrive: one confessing to his murder, one promising 'the rest at the anniversary dinner.' As Kestrel traces the forged document through Merrick's fractured family and a vanished housekeeper, she realizes the killer is someone with access to the original case file — someone inside the investigation, or inside her own firm. At the anniversary dinner, Kestrel springs a trap using the will's impossible date as bait; the confessor is exposed as Merrick's daughter, who killed him to stop him disinheriting her — but the second letter's author, the housekeeper, chose Kestrel precisely because she once buried a similar truth of her own. In the end, Kestrel files the will as invalid, keeps the confession out of court, and finally confronts the memory she has spent her career outrunning.
about_author: Lior Hartwell is a former probate clerk turned novelist who spent a decade watching families unravel over paper. They write mysteries about the documents people leave behind and the ones they wish they could destroy.

chapters.title: The Will That Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: Kestrel Villalobos opens probate on Aldous Merrick's estate and finds a will dated after his death, naming her executor. Her POV establishes her meticulous control and a flicker of unease about her own past cases. The emotional beat: professional confidence cracking into dread as the impossible document lands in her hands.

chapters.title: Two Envelopes
chapters.summary: Twin letters arrive — one confessing to Merrick's murder, one promising 'the rest' at the anniversary dinner, addressed in handwriting Kestrel almost recognizes. Her POV alternates with a cold, unnamed observer reviewing a case file. The beat: fascination curdling into fear as she realizes she was chosen deliberately.

chapters.title: The Family Tree Has Roots
chapters.summary: Kestrel interviews the Merrick heirs: brittle daughter Camille, estranged son Theo, and a widow who seems relieved rather than grieving. Each knows details of the death certificate they shouldn't. Kestrel's POV; the beat is the slow discovery that everyone is performing innocence, and one performance is too polished.

chapters.title: What the File Remembers
chapters.summary: Digging into the original investigation, Kestrel finds pages missing from the case file — pages only investigators or her own firm could have pulled. A flashback surfaces her own buried secret: a truth she falsified years ago to protect a client. The beat: guilt sharpening into resolve; she can't judge others without judging herself.

chapters.title: The Housekeeper's Room
chapters.summary: Kestrel tracks Marisol Vega, Merrick's vanished housekeeper, to a coastal boarding house. Marisol admits she witnessed something the night Merrick died but refuses to say what — and reveals she wrote one of the letters. Kestrel's POV with Marisol's guarded counterpoint. The beat: an alliance offered and distrusted.

chapters.title: Anniversary Preparations
chapters.summary: Camille announces a lavish one-year memorial dinner and pressures Kestrel to read the will aloud there. Meanwhile Theo threatens to contest everything, and the anonymous observer's chapters close in: they know Kestrel's office, her habits, her old mistake. The beat: the walls tightening, time running out toward the dinner.

chapters.title: A Forgery of Grief
chapters.summary: A forensic examiner confirms the will's signature was traced from a hospital consent form — signed by someone at Merrick's deathbed. Kestrel realizes the forger had access to both the dying man and her firm's records. Her POV, spiraling between suspicion of Theo, Camille, and her own junior partner. The beat: paranoia as every ally becomes a suspect.

chapters.title: The Second Letter Opens
chapters.summary: Marisol sends Kestrel the missing file pages: Merrick was poisoned slowly, over months, by someone managing his medication. Kestrel matches the prescription trail to Camille — but the letter's phrasing echoes language from her own old case, meaning the writer knows her secret intimately. The beat: horror that the trap may be set for her, not by her.

chapters.title: The Anniversary Dinner
chapters.summary: At the dinner, Kestrel reads the will and announces its fatal flaw — the impossible date — daring the forger to defend it. Camille takes the bait, revealing intimate knowledge of the deathbed, then breaks when Kestrel produces the prescription records. Marisol watches from the back; the observer's identity snaps into focus. The beat: climax — public unmasking, glass raised, truth spilled like wine.

chapters.title: Kestrel and the Confession
chapters.summary: In the aftermath, Kestrel learns Marisol wrote the second letter to force Kestrel — the lawyer who once buried a similar truth — into doing right this time. Kestrel files the will as invalid, hands the evidence to police, and chooses to report her own old transgression rather than repeat the pattern. Final beat: loyalty to truth over self, memory faced at last.
